title: Unit 1d - Algorithms and Runtime
summary: Title slide introducing the Algorithms and Runtime unit for CS 103, presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 1d of CS 103, covering Algorithms and Runtime. The unit explores what algorithms are, how they are represented, and how we measure their efficiency using runtime analysis and big-O notation. Topics include algorithm definitions, pseudocode, searching algorithms (sequential and binary search), sorting algorithms (bubble sort), and time complexity classification.
notes_text: This unit is foundational for understanding computational efficiency. Students should pay attention to how different algorithms solve the same problem with vastly different performance characteristics.

title: Algorithms
summary: Defines algorithms informally and formally, emphasizing their key properties: ordered, unambiguous, executable, and terminating steps.
main_text: Algorithms are at the heart of computer systems, both in hardware (HW) and software (SW). They are fundamental to Computer Science and Computer Engineering. Informal definition: An algorithm is a precise way to accomplish a task or solve a problem. A more formal definition: An ordered set of unambiguous, executable steps that defines a terminating process. Key properties of algorithms include: Ordered - the steps of an algorithm have a particular order, not just any order. Unambiguous - each step is completely clear as to what is to be done. Executable - each step can actually be performed. Terminating Process - the algorithm will stop eventually (sometimes this requirement is relaxed). Examples of everyday algorithms include brushing your teeth and calculating your GPA.
notes_text: The distinction between informal and formal definitions is important. The formal definition's four properties (ordered, unambiguous, executable, terminating) serve as criteria for determining whether a set of instructions qualifies as an algorithm. The terminating requirement is sometimes relaxed for processes like operating systems that run indefinitely.

images.description: An inset box listing the four key properties of algorithms: Ordered, Unambiguous, Executable, and Terminating Process, each with a brief explanation.

title: Algorithm Representation
summary: Explains that algorithms are language-independent and can be represented as flow charts, pseudocode, or specific program implementations.
main_text: An algorithm focuses on how to solve a problem regardless of the language or specific implementation. An algorithm is NOT a program NOR tied to one programming language. Just as a story may be represented as a book, movie, or spoken by a story-teller, an algorithm may be represented in many ways. Common representations include: Flow chart - a visual diagram showing the steps and decision points. Pseudocode - English-like syntax using primitives that most programming languages would have. A specific program implementation in a given programming language like C++. The key insight is that the algorithm is the abstract solution method, separate from any particular way of writing it down.
notes_text: Understanding the distinction between an algorithm and a program is crucial. An algorithm is the conceptual solution strategy, while a program is a concrete implementation in a specific language. This distinction allows computer scientists to analyze and compare algorithms independently of hardware or language considerations.

title: Pseudocode Primitives
summary: Introduces the three fundamental pseudocode constructs: assignment, conditionals (selection), and loops (repetition).
main_text: Pseudocode uses three fundamental primitives to express algorithms. Assignment: name <- expression, where name is a descriptive name/variable and expression describes the value to be associated with name. Select one of two possible choices (conditionals): 'if (condition) then (activity) else (activity)' or 'if (condition) then (activity)' for one-way selection. Repeated execution of statements (loops): 'while (condition) do (activity)' executes as long as condition is true. 'repeat (activity) until (condition)' executes at least once then checks condition. 'foreach name in (set / collection) do (activity)' iterates over each element in a set or collection. These three primitives - assignment, selection, and iteration - form the building blocks of all algorithms expressed in pseudocode.
notes_text: These three constructs correspond to the fundamental control structures in virtually all programming languages. The left arrow (<-) notation for assignment distinguishes pseudocode from languages that use the equals sign. Understanding these primitives is essential for reading and writing algorithms throughout the course.

title: Algorithms and Runtime
summary: Introduces runtime analysis and big-O notation for classifying algorithm efficiency from constant O(1) to exponential O(2^n) time.
main_text: There may be many algorithms for solving the same problem. How do we judge which is more efficient? Efficiency may refer to time (speed), amount of memory used, or even how much power is consumed. This unit focuses on time. Typically, we classify algorithms into bins based on how their run-time scales with an input of size n, using something called big-O notation. The common runtime classifications from fastest to slowest are: O(1) - Constant time (independent of n). O(log n) - Logarithmic time. O(n) - Linear time. O(n * log n) - Log-Linear time. O(n^2) - Quadratic time. O(n^3) - Cubic time. O(2^n) - Exponential time. These classifications help us understand how an algorithm's performance will change as the input size grows.
notes_text: The big-O classification spectrum is one of the most important concepts in computer science. As input size n grows, the differences between these classes become dramatic. An O(n) algorithm might handle millions of inputs easily, while an O(2^n) algorithm becomes impractical for even modest input sizes. The diagram shows an algorithm being classified into one of these bins.

images.description: A classification diagram showing an algorithm being sorted into one of seven big-O runtime bins, with arrows from 'an algorithm' pointing down to each category from O(1) through O(2^n).

title: Algorithm Example 1 - Finding Factors
summary: Demonstrates a factor-finding algorithm using pseudocode with a basic O(n) approach and an improved O(sqrt(n)) optimization.
main_text: Problem: List/print all factors of a natural number n. How would you check if a number is a factor of n? Use the remainder (modulo) operation. What is the range of possible factors? From 1 to n. Basic algorithm: i <- 1, while(i <= n) do: if (remainder of n/i is zero) then list i as a factor of n, i <- i+1. This checks every number from 1 to n, making it O(n). An improvement: Since factors come in pairs (if i is a factor, then n/i is also a factor), we only need to check up to the square root of n. Improved algorithm: i <- 1, while(i <= ____) do: if (remainder of n/i is zero) then list i and ____ as a factor of n, i <- i+1. Examples shown: factors of 8 are 1,2,4,8; factors of 12 are 1,2,3,4,6,12; factors of 24 are 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24; factors of 36 are 1,2,3,4,6,6,9,12,18,36.
notes_text: This example illustrates how understanding mathematical properties (factor pairs) can lead to more efficient algorithms. The blanks are intentionally left for students to fill in: the loop condition should be i <= sqrt(n), and the second factor listed should be n/i. Notice how factors come in pairs that multiply to n.

images.description: A table showing the complete factor lists for numbers 8, 12, 24, and 36, demonstrating how factors come in pairs.

title: Algorithm Time Complexity
summary: Explains how algorithms are judged by runtime for a given input size n, using worst-case analysis independent of hardware.
main_text: We often judge algorithms by how long they take to run for a given input size, n. Algorithms often have different run-times based on the input size. For example, n equals the number of elements in a list to search or sort. Different input patterns can lead to best-case and worst-case times. Average-case times can be helpful. But we usually use worst case times for comparison purposes. We also want to be able to compare the time an algorithm takes in a way that is independent of the computer running it. The same algorithm might run a lot faster on a server than your phone due to the hardware. This motivates the need for an abstract measure of efficiency that focuses on how the number of operations scales with input size, rather than actual wall-clock time.
notes_text: Worst-case analysis provides a guarantee: the algorithm will never perform worse than this bound. This is particularly important in real-time systems or safety-critical applications. Hardware independence is achieved by counting operations rather than measuring time in seconds.

title: Calculating Runtime
summary: Shows how to calculate runtime by counting steps of work in pseudocode, deriving an expression in terms of input size n.
main_text: Given an input to an algorithm of size n, we start by deriving an expression (in terms of n) for the steps of work an algorithm performs, usually for its WORST CASE run time. Just walk the code and count up 'steps' of work. It is fine if what we call a 'step' of work is a bit imprecise because we will usually apply big-O notation (see next slide). Example pseudocode for finding factors: i <- 1, while(i <= n) do: if (n mod i == 0) then list i as a factor of n, i <- i+1. In this algorithm, the initialization takes 1 step, the while loop condition is checked n times, the modulo and comparison inside the loop each execute n times, and the increment executes n times. The total work is proportional to n.
notes_text: The key technique is to identify the loop and determine how many times it executes in the worst case. Each operation inside the loop contributes a constant amount of work per iteration. The total is the number of iterations multiplied by the work per iteration, plus any constant startup/cleanup work.

images.description: A code box showing the factor-finding pseudocode: i <- 1, while(i <= n) do, if (n mod i == 0) then list i as a factor of n, i <- i+1.
labels: List i as a factor of n

title: Applying Big-O Notation
summary: Explains how to derive big-O by keeping only the dominant term and discarding constants, with a worked example showing O(5n+1) = O(n).
main_text: From the expression, we find the corresponding big-O expression for that runtime by assuming n is LARGE (approaching infinity) and thus we: Only keep the dominant term in the expression. Discard constant coefficients. The result is the big-O (worst-case or upper-bound) run-time. Example: If an algorithm with input size of n runs in 3n^2 + 10n + 1000 steps, we say that it runs in O(n^2) because if n is large, 3n^2 will dominate the other terms. Detailed step count for the factor-finding algorithm: i <- 1 costs 1 step, while(i <= n) do costs 1*n, if (n mod i == 0) then costs 2*n (modulo and compare are 2 ops), List i as a factor of n costs 1*n, i <- i+1 costs 1*n. Total: 5n+1. O(5n+1) = O(n). Big-O notation lets us express the amount of work an algorithm performs in a way that doesn't require exact precision but helps us compare the efficiency of different algorithms.
notes_text: The two rules for simplifying to big-O are essential: drop lower-order terms and drop constant coefficients. This works because for sufficiently large n, the highest-order term dominates. For example, when n = 1000, 3n^2 = 3,000,000 while 10n = 10,000 and 1000 is negligible. The annotation on the code shows how to count 2 ops for the modulo and compare operations.

images.description: An annotated code box showing the factor-finding algorithm with step counts labeled on the right side: 1 for initialization, 1*n for while check, 2*n for modulo and compare, 1*n for listing, 1*n for increment, totaling 5n+1 which simplifies to O(n).

title: Algorithm Example 1 - Runtime Comparison
summary: Compares the basic O(n) factor-finding algorithm with the improved O(sqrt(n)) version that only checks up to the square root.
main_text: List/print all factors of a natural number, n. What is a factor? What is the range of possible factors? Basic algorithm: i <- 1, while(i <= n) do: if (remainder of n/i is zero) then list i as a factor of n, i <- i+1. This has runtime O(n) because the loop runs n times. An improvement: i <- 1, while(i <= sqrt(n)) do: if (remainder of n/i is zero) then list i and n/i as a factor of n, i <- i+1. This improved version has runtime O(sqrt(n)) because the loop only runs up to the square root of n. By recognizing that factors come in pairs (i and n/i), we can cut the search space dramatically. For n = 1,000,000, the basic version checks 1,000,000 values while the improved version only checks 1,000.
notes_text: This is an excellent example of algorithmic optimization. The mathematical insight that factors come in pairs allows us to reduce the number of iterations from n to sqrt(n). This demonstrates that understanding the problem domain can lead to significantly better algorithms without changing the fundamental approach.

title: Algorithm Example 2a - Sequential Search
summary: Introduces sequential (linear) search on an ordered list, showing pseudocode and explaining best case (1 step) and worst case (n steps).
main_text: Problem: Searching an ordered list (array) for a specific value, k, and return its index or -1 if it is not in the list. Option 1: Sequential Search. Start at first item, check if it is equal to k, repeat for second, third, fourth item, etc. Best Case: Find it right away (1 step). Worst Case: Not present in the list (n steps). Pseudocode: i <- 0, while (i < length(List)) do: if (List[i] equal to k) then return i, else i <- i+1. return -1. The algorithm starts at index 0 and moves through the list one element at a time. If it finds k, it returns the index. If it reaches the end without finding k, it returns -1 to indicate the value was not found. Example: searching for k=12 in the list [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 15, 19] at indices 0 through 8.
notes_text: Sequential search is the simplest search algorithm and works on both ordered and unordered lists. Its simplicity is its advantage, but its O(n) worst-case performance makes it inefficient for large datasets. The example shows a sorted list, which sets up the motivation for binary search on the next slide.

images.description: An array diagram showing a list with values [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 15, 19] at indices 0 through 8, with k=12 as the search target.

title: Algorithm Example 2b - Binary Search Introduction
summary: Introduces binary search, which exploits sorted order by comparing with the middle element and eliminating half the list each step.
main_text: Sequential search does NOT take advantage of the ordered nature of the list. It would work the same (equally well) on an ordered or unordered list. Binary Search takes advantage of an ordered list by comparing k with the middle element and based on the result, ruling out all numbers greater or smaller, then repeating with the middle element of the remaining list. Example walkthrough searching for k=6 in list [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 15, 19]: Step 1 - Start in middle at index 4 (value 9). Compare: 6 < 9, so eliminate the right half. Step 2 - Look at middle of remaining left portion at index 1 (value 3). Compare: 6 > 4 (value at the midpoint of the left subarray). Step 3 - Narrow down further until 6 = 6 is found. Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements.
notes_text: Binary search is a classic divide-and-conquer algorithm. The key prerequisite is that the list must be sorted. The visual walkthrough demonstrates how each comparison halves the search space, which is what gives binary search its logarithmic runtime. Students should trace through the example carefully to understand the elimination process.

images.description: A step-by-step visual trace of binary search for k=6 in the array [2,3,4,6,9,10,13,15,19], showing three stages where the search space is halved each time by comparing with the middle element. Highlighted cells show the current middle element being compared.

title: Algorithm Example 2b - Binary Search Implementation
summary: Provides complete binary search pseudocode using start/end pointers and demonstrates a full trace searching for k=11.
main_text: Binary Search implementation: Compare k with middle element of list and if not equal, rule out half of the list and repeat on the other half. Implementation uses a range of searchable elements defined as [start, end) where start is inclusive and end is exclusive. Pseudocode: start <- 0; end <- length(List); while (start != end) do: i <- (start + end) / 2; if (k == List[i]) then return i; else if (k > List[i]) then start <- i+1; else end <- i; return -1. Example trace for k=11 in list [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 11, 13, 15, 19]: Initially start=0, end=9, i=4. Since 11 > 9 (List[4]), set start=5. Now start=5, end=9, i=7. Since 11 < 15 (List[7]), set end=7. Now start=5, end=7, i=6. Since 11 < 13 (List[6]), set end=6. Now start=5, end=6, i=5. 11 == 11 (List[5]), return 5.
notes_text: The half-open interval [start, end) is a common convention in computer science where start is inclusive and end is exclusive. This simplifies boundary conditions. The trace shows four comparisons to find the element in a list of 9 items, compared to potentially 9 comparisons with sequential search. Notice how start and end converge toward the target.

images.description: A detailed step-by-step trace of binary search for k=11, showing four stages of the array [2,3,4,6,9,11,13,15,19] with start, end, and i pointers converging on the target element at index 5.

title: Complexity of Search Algorithms
summary: Analyzes sequential search as O(n) and begins deriving binary search complexity by tracking how the list halves each iteration.
main_text: Sequential Search on a list of length n: Worst case requires searching through the entire list. Time complexity = an + k, where a is some constant for the number of operations performed in the loop as we iterate, and k is some constant representing startup/finish work outside the loop. Sequential Search = O(n) after dropping constants. Binary Search on a list of length n: Worst case requires continually dividing the list in two until we reach a sublist of size 1. After iteration 1, n/2 items remain. After iteration 2, n/4 items remain. After iteration 3, n/8 items remain. After iteration k, n/2^k items remain. We stop when n/2^k = 1. Solving for k gives the number of iterations needed. The blanks are left for students to fill in: Time = a*log_2(n) + k = O(log_2(n)).
notes_text: This slide sets up the derivation of binary search's O(log n) runtime. The table showing remaining items after each iteration is key to understanding why the runtime is logarithmic. Each iteration halves the remaining search space, so after k iterations, n/2^k items remain. Setting n/2^k = 1 and solving for k gives k = log_2(n). Students should work through this derivation.

images.description: A table showing remaining items after each binary search iteration: iteration 1 leaves n/2, iteration 2 leaves n/4, iteration 3 leaves n/8, iteration k leaves n/2^k, and the final iteration leaves 1 item. Below: Solve n/2^k = 1, k = ___ iterations.

title: Complexity of Search Algorithms - Solution
summary: Completes the derivation showing sequential search is O(n) and binary search is O(log_2 n), with a graph comparing their growth rates.
main_text: Sequential Search on a list of length n: Worst case requires searching through entire list. Time complexity = an + k. Sequential Search = O(n). Binary Search on a list of length n: Worst case requires continually dividing the list in two until we reach a sublist of size 1. Time = a*log_2(n) + k = O(log_2 n). The derivation: After iteration 1, n/2 items remain. After iteration 2, n/4 items remain. After iteration 3, n/8 items remain. After iteration k, n/2^k items remain. Solving n/2^k = 1 gives k = log_2(n) iterations. As n gets large, binary search is far more efficient than sequential search. For a list of 1 billion items, sequential search may need 1 billion comparisons while binary search needs only about 30.
notes_text: The graph on this slide dramatically illustrates the difference between O(n) and O(log n). The linear function grows steadily while the logarithmic function flattens out. This visual reinforcement helps students appreciate why algorithm choice matters so much for large inputs. Binary search requires the list to be sorted, which is a tradeoff worth considering.

images.description: A graph comparing the runtime growth of sequential search (linear, steep line) versus binary search (logarithmic, nearly flat curve) as N increases from 0 to 50, with runtime on the y-axis from 0 to 50.
A table showing remaining items after each binary search iteration, with the solution: k = log_2(n) iterations.

title: Sorting Algorithms
summary: Motivates sorting as a prerequisite for binary search and introduces bubble sort as a simple but inefficient sorting algorithm.
main_text: If we have an unordered list, sequential search becomes our only choice since binary search requires a sorted list. If we will perform a lot of searches, it may be beneficial to sort the list (to make it ordered), then use binary search. The one-time cost of sorting can be amortized over many fast binary searches, making the overall process more efficient. Many sorting algorithms exist with varying run-time efficiencies. Bubble sort is a simple, though not terribly efficient algorithm. More advanced sorting algorithms like Quicksort and Mergesort offer better performance. The choice of whether to sort first depends on how many searches will be performed on the data.
notes_text: This slide bridges the searching and sorting topics. The key insight is the tradeoff between sorting cost and search efficiency. If you only search once, sequential search on an unsorted list is fine. But if you search many times, paying the upfront cost to sort enables much faster binary searches. This cost-benefit analysis is a common pattern in algorithm design.

title: Bubble Sort Algorithm
summary: Explains bubble sort mechanics with C++ code and a visual trace showing how adjacent elements are compared and swapped across multiple passes.
main_text: Bubble sort performs several passes over the data. Variable i tracks the stopping point for each pass. Variable j starts at the beginning of the array, moves sequentially and compares its element with its immediate neighbor. C++ implementation: void bsort(int mylist[], int size) { int i, j; for(i=...) { for(j=...) { if(mylist[j] > mylist[j+1]) { // swap mylist[j] & mylist[j+1] } } } }. Visual trace of Pass 1 with n-1 comparisons on array [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1]: Compare 7 and 3, swap to get [3, 7, 8, 6, 5, 1]. Compare 7 and 8, no swap. Compare 8 and 6, swap to get [3, 7, 6, 8, 5, 1]. Compare 8 and 5, swap. Compare 8 and 1, swap to get [3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 8]. After Pass 1, the largest element (8) has 'bubbled up' to the end. Pass 2 performs n-2 comparisons on the remaining unsorted portion.
notes_text: The name 'bubble sort' comes from the way larger elements 'bubble up' to the end of the array with each pass. Each pass guarantees that the next largest unsorted element reaches its correct position. The visual trace is essential for understanding the algorithm's mechanics. Notice the for loop bounds are left as exercises for students to fill in.

images.description: A step-by-step visual trace of bubble sort Pass 1 and the beginning of Pass 2 on the array [7,3,8,6,5,1], showing j and i pointer positions, swap/no-swap decisions at each step, with the largest element (8) bubbling to the end after Pass 1.

title: Bubble Sort - Work Analysis (Blank)
summary: Presents bubble sort with blank step counts for each pass, asking students to determine the total work and big-O complexity.
main_text: Bubble Sort is simple though not terribly efficient. On each pass through the list, pick up the maximum element and place it at the end of the list. Then repeat using a list of size n-1 (without the newly placed maximum value). How much total work is required? Starting with the array [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1]: Pass 1 produces [3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 2 produces [3, 5, 1, 6, 7, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 3 produces [3, 1, 5, 6, 7, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 4 produces [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 5 produces [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 6 with ____ steps. The total complexity is O(____). Students are expected to fill in the step counts and derive the overall big-O.
notes_text: This is the exercise version of the slide where students work through the analysis themselves. Each pass performs a decreasing number of comparisons: Pass 1 does n-1 comparisons, Pass 2 does n-2, and so on down to 1. The total is the sum (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2, which simplifies to O(n^2).

images.description: A visual trace showing the original array [7,3,8,6,5,1] and the state after each of 6 passes, with blank step counts for students to fill in and a blank O(___) for the final complexity.

title: Bubble Sort - Work Analysis (Solution)
summary: Reveals that bubble sort requires n, n-1, n-2, ... steps per pass, totaling n(n+1)/2 operations, giving O(n^2) complexity.
main_text: Bubble Sort is simple though not terribly efficient. On each pass through the list, pick up the maximum element and place it at the end of the list. Then repeat using a list of size n-1. Solution for the work at each pass starting with array [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1]: Pass 1 takes n steps (5 comparisons for 6 elements), producing [3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 8]. Pass 2 takes n-1 steps, producing [3, 5, 1, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 3 takes n-2 steps, producing [3, 1, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 4 takes ... steps, producing [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 5 takes 2 steps. Pass 6 takes 1 step. The total work is the sum: (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 2 + 1. The overall runtime complexity is O(n^2).
notes_text: The sum (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 equals n(n-1)/2 using the arithmetic series formula. Applying big-O simplification: n(n-1)/2 = (n^2 - n)/2. Dropping the lower order term and constant gives O(n^2). This quadratic growth makes bubble sort impractical for large datasets.

images.description: A visual trace showing the array state after each pass with filled-in step counts: Pass 1 (n steps), Pass 2 (n-1 steps), Pass 3 (n-2 steps), Pass 4 (... steps), Pass 5 (2 steps), Pass 6 (1 step), with O(n^2) shown as the final answer.

title: Complexity of Sort Algorithms
summary: Compares bubble sort O(n^2) with advanced sorts like Quicksort and Mergesort at O(n*log n), with a graph showing the dramatic difference.
main_text: Bubble Sort uses 2 nested loops. Execute outer loop n-1 times. For each outer loop iteration, inner loop runs i times. Time complexity is proportional to: n-1 + n-2 + n-3 + ... + 3 + 2 + 1 = (n^2 + n)/2 = O(n^2). Other sort algorithms (Quicksort, Mergesort, etc.) can run in O(n*log_2 n). The difference between O(n^2) and O(n*log n) is dramatic for large inputs. For example, with n = 1,000,000: bubble sort requires roughly 10^12 operations while quicksort requires roughly 2 * 10^7 operations, a factor of 50,000 times faster. The graph comparing N, N^2, and N*log_2(N) shows that while N^2 grows rapidly (reaching 400 at N=20), N*log_2(N) grows much more moderately.
notes_text: This slide provides the capstone comparison for the sorting section. The graph visually demonstrates why O(n^2) algorithms are impractical for large datasets. Quicksort and Mergesort achieve O(n log n) through divide-and-conquer strategies that will be studied in more advanced courses. The key takeaway is that algorithm choice has enormous practical impact on performance.

images.description: A graph comparing three growth functions: N (linear, bottom), N*log_2(N) (moderate growth, middle), and N^2 (steep parabolic growth, top) for N from 0 to 20, with runtime values on the y-axis up to 400.

title: Common Algorithm Runtimes
summary: Summarizes all seven big-O runtime classes with example algorithms and code snippets for constant, cubic, and exponential cases.
main_text: Common algorithm runtimes from fastest to slowest: O(1) Constant - Example: Simple conversions. Code example using quadratic formula: cin >> a >> b >> c; double det = b*b - 4*a*c; compute x1 and x2. Uses formula x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a. O(log n) Logarithmic - Example: Binary Search. O(n) Linear - Example: Sequential Search, Neural Network Back-propagation. O(n * log n) Log-Linear - Example: Quicksort, Mergesort, Heapsort. O(n^2) Quadratic - Example: Bubble sort, Image convolution. O(n^3) Cubic - Example: Matrix Multiply. Code: for(int i=0; i<N; i++) for(int j=0; j<N; j++) { C[i][j]=0; for(int k=0; k<N; k++) C[i][j] += A[i][k]*B[k][j]; }. O(2^n) Exponential - Example: Many Combinatoric or Optimization algorithms, Subset Sums. Problem: Does any subset of inputs add or subtract equal to N given 37 192 42 7 3 86 102 91. In general, focus on nested loops to help determine runtime.
notes_text: This is a comprehensive reference slide. The constant time example shows the quadratic formula which requires a fixed number of operations regardless of input. The cubic example demonstrates three nested loops for matrix multiplication. The exponential example (subset sums) shows a problem where every possible combination must potentially be checked. The key heuristic: count the depth of nested loops to estimate runtime.

images.description: A comprehensive table showing seven runtime classes (O(1) through O(2^n)) with their names (Constant through Exponential) and example algorithms, plus three code snippets illustrating constant (quadratic formula), cubic (matrix multiply), and exponential (subset sums) complexity.

title: Importance of Time Complexity
summary: Explains why time complexity matters: it determines whether problems are efficient, possible, or impossible to solve in practice.
main_text: Time complexity makes the difference between efficient, possible, and impossible. Many important problems currently can only be solved with exponential run-time algorithms (e.g. O(2^n) time). No known polynomial-time algorithm exists for these problems. Usually, algorithms are only practical if they run in polynomial time (O(n^k) for some constant k). A comparison table shows how different complexities scale with input size N: For N=2: O(1)=1, O(log_2 n)=1, O(n)=2, O(n*log_2 n)=2, O(n^2)=4, O(2^n)=4. For N=20: O(1)=1, O(log_2 n)=4.3, O(n)=20, O(n*log_2 n)=86.4, O(n^2)=400, O(2^n)=1,048,576. For N=200: O(1)=1, O(log_2 n)=7.6, O(n)=200, O(n*log_2 n)=1528.8, O(n^2)=40,000, O(2^n)=1.60694E+60. For N=2000: O(1)=1, O(log_2 n)=11.0, O(n)=2000, O(n*log_2 n)=21,931.6, O(n^2)=4,000,000, O(2^n)=#NUM! (overflow, too large to compute).
notes_text: The table powerfully illustrates why exponential algorithms are impractical. At N=200, O(2^n) produces a number with 60 digits, and at N=2000 it overflows entirely. Meanwhile O(log n) barely grows at all. This connects to the famous P vs NP problem in computer science: whether problems solvable in exponential time can be solved in polynomial time. This remains one of the greatest open questions in mathematics and computer science.

images.description: A comparison table showing the computed values for six complexity classes (O(1), O(log_2 n), O(n), O(n*log_2 n), O(n^2), O(2^n)) at four input sizes (N=2, 20, 200, 2000), dramatically showing how exponential growth becomes impossibly large while logarithmic growth stays manageable.
